prize_parts.citation: For showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting drive reallocation across firms and shape the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B048 with Melitz and Helpman as a single prize part. I judge it by how well the central claims have survived testing, not by influence alone. Melitz (2003) is an identifiable originating model. It replaced the representative firm with selection into exporting and within-industry reallocation, and it generated predictions that could fail: exporter productivity premia, selection into export markets, and reallocation after liberalisation. These have been checked across many countries and datasets over more than twenty years, and the qualitative patterns have held. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, together with his earlier trade theory, makes him the natural second name. The exchange sharpened my view on two points. First, the citation should be worded around the selection-and-reallocation mechanism and the gains-from-trade channel, not around the whole firm-level trade literature. That is the best available response to the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question. Second, Helpman's separate appearance in a trade-politics package outside this shortlist is a reason to define the citation tightly and avoid double-counting. It is not a reason to discount his claim here, because the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work is part of this discovery. My confidence is somewhat higher than in round 1, but only because colleagues' arguments on attribution and identification were specific. The number of members now preferring B048 is not scientific evidence, and I do not count it as such. On the chair's question about what counts as evidence, I would treat thematic overlap with recent prizes as at most a marginal-novelty or attribution consideration. The 2008 prize and field rotation are timing considerations, not evidence about merit.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main weakness. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely parallel firm-level facts and models and are outside the ballot entry. A two-name credit could therefore be read as favouring the theory over the empirical foundations, and the three-name cap cannot fix that. A citation limited to the mechanism reduces the problem but does not remove it. The magnitude of the welfare gains depends on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, so the prize would rest on the qualitative reframing and the empirical toolkit, not on settled quantitative estimates. Redding's quantitative work is a later strand that I still leave out, and that is a judgement call. Finally, I rely on my own recollection of the literature, and I have not independently verified any source.

responses.point: Friberg keeps B001 first with moderate confidence. He argues that its lasting contribution is the systematic cross-country data on investor protection and ownership and the question it made central, which do not depend on every causal legal-origins claim. He concedes that B001 would not compete on identification strength and lists B048 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about identification, and I agree that field-creating influence is real. My difficulty is that the coding critiques raised by colleagues, including the anti-director index, concern the measurement of the data itself. The data contribution is therefore not insulated from the contested part in the way a purely causal reading would be. Critique generated by a literature is evidence of influence. It is not by itself evidence that the central claims held up, and I separate those two when I assess maturity. In a head-to-head comparison, even on a citation resting on the data and research design, I would still choose B048. The cleaner two-name attribution matters, and so does the stronger record of predictions tested against micro-data. What would move me is a citation wording, and a short list of specific regularities, that colleagues can show are robust to re-coding and to the law-versus-history question. I have not seen that demonstrated in this exchange.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, keeps B001 slightly ahead of B048. He would word the citation around legal institutions and investor protection being measurable and co-varying with financial outcomes, not around legal origin as a proven cause. He calls the gap with B048 small, and he concedes that Vishny's exclusion is a real attribution cost.
responses.response: His proposed wording is the right way to avoid endorsing the strong causal claim, and it makes B001 more defensible than a citation built on legal origin. It also shows what the discovery would then be: a measurable association and a research agenda. That is a weaker claim than selection into exporting, which is a specific mechanism with specific predictions that could have failed and did not. I read his own concession on Vishny as adding to this, since the cost falls on the original papers. I also take his point that creating a field can be more decisive than refining one, and it is why I do not dismiss B001. But I would rate the claim that survived testing above the claim that was influential, and so I keep B048 ahead. I see the gap as real but not large.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B037 (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler). He treats Kiyotaki and Moore as the unambiguous core and would accept a two-name version. He argues that the 2022 prize overlap reduces marginal novelty but is not disqualifying, since collateral amplification in general equilibrium differs from banking and crisis origins.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap is not disqualifying. That is why B037 is my first alternative and not a lower one. I also welcome his willingness to accept a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version. It resolves much of my concern about Gertler's credit being split with the New Keynesian entry and entangled with the accelerator lineage. Where I still differ is on evidence. By his own account, the empirical identification of collateral channels is harder and more mixed than the theory's influence suggests. A citation worded around the amplification mechanism avoids overclaiming, but the case then rests on conceptual and modelling impact. For that reason I rank B048 first, where core predictions have been tested repeatedly. If the committee cannot settle B048's attribution question, I would see a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize as the cleanest fallback among my alternatives.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson supports B048 and calls the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line the real vulnerability, because it concerns priority on the empirical foundations and not just a later extension. She would draft the citation around the selection mechanism and the gains-from-trade framework so that it does not overclaim the firm-level facts.
responses.response: I agree with her framing and I have adopted her drafting approach in my citation. This also speaks to the chair's first question. If the committee judges the priority question material, a mechanism-limited citation is sufficient for me, and it does not change my preference between B048 and B001 or B015. If the committee decided instead that a two-name credit is unfair to the empirical line, I would count that as a genuine cost and not dismiss it. My alternatives do not escape comparable attribution problems: Vishny and the legal-origins critique for B001, and the Katz and Dorn choice for B015. So I would still not conclude that B048 should lose ground to them on attribution grounds alone.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from B015 to B048 in round 1. He acknowledged that my narrower Autor-Hanson credit for B015 shows how hard that candidate is to define, and he holds that the attribution problem is real and not just a matter of taste.
responses.response: I accept his reading. I still rate B015 highly on identification, which is why it remains my second alternative. It is also why I would only support it with the narrowest credit I can defend, Autor and Hanson, which leaves out the technology strand and Dorn. That narrowness is the cost, and I do not want to cover it up. In answer to the chair's question, I do not see a three-name B015 citation that is both coherent and clear of the 2023 and 2024 labour and technology prizes. I would not use that overlap as a merit argument. I would use it only as a reason that the credit structure is less settled than B048's.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question as material, which a two-name credit on this ballot entry cannot resolve.
How much of the gains-from-trade result depends on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, and whether this weakens the claim to a robust discovery.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial work should be treated as part of this discovery or as a later separable one.
How Helpman's separate appearance in a trade-politics package affects framing and credit, and whether tight citation wording is enough.

Whether B001 survives scrutiny better than I currently judge. I weigh the coding and causal-identification critiques heavily, as a metascience researcher, and I may be underweighting field-creating influence.
My assessments rely on my own knowledge of the literature and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Melitz, Helpman or Redding is documented in my supplied profile, and none to the credited names on my alternatives B037 and B015. My profile does record Harvard appointments from 2006 to 2017 and a Harvard evolutionary-dynamics network. It also records close co-authorship with Magnus Johannesson, a former committee member, and SSE ties to Tore Ellingsen, none of which is a candidate connection. My work on replication and metascience, including the Institute for Replication, shapes how heavily I weigh robustness and testing against influence. I disclose that as a perspective that could bias me against B001, which I ranked seventh, and I have tried to apply the same criteria to every field. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
